newsitem.title: USA: G-3 seen looking to limit additional dollar gains.
newsitem.headline: G-3 seen looking to limit additional dollar gains.

text.p: Despite repeated pleas from French officials to strengthen the dollar's value, their big brothers in the Group of Seven nations seem unwilling to let the dollar rally much further, U.S. analysts said.
They said the greenback has already climbed to levels that trouble officials in Germany, Japan and the United States, where opposition to fresh dollar gains should limit further upside.

"We've had a lot of volatility lately because of the switch to emphasizing European depreciation, not yen depreciation. In terms of overall action, the dollar is likely to stay in a relatively narrow range," said Tim McGee, international economist at Tokai Bank.
France is wistfully eyeing a weaker franc as a way to boost exports as its anemic economy threatens to derail the proposed European Monetary Union (EMU) launch in 1999.
But analysts said the Germans seem reluctant to allow the mark to weaken past 1.60 to the dollar, which now stands near 1.56 marks.

"It sounds like the Germans would be comfortable to see the dollar in a 1.58 to 1.60 mark range. We could see 1.60 between now and next June," said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Using the 3.38 mark/franc parity rate in Europe's floating Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a 1.60 dollar/mark rate only gets dollar/franc to 5.40, well below the 6.0 rate some French officials are said to desire.
With the Bundesbank expected to hold German interest rates steady in coming months, French leaders must look to other means besides monetary policy to spark economic growth, analysts said.
While Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet has asserted he sees no case for devaluing the franc, analysts said the temptation was clear in the comments of other French leaders.

"For a long time it seemed the French had finally recognized the benefit of tying the franc to the mark and importing German financial stability. But we can no longer take it for granted that they won't devalue," said Gabriele Lamers, international economist at Bank of Boston.

Faster U.S. economic growth or higher U.S. interest rates could help the dollar move to 1.65 marks in coming months, analysts said. That would push dollar/franc to about 5.58, but would severely test the patience of Bundesbank officials.
"I think the Bundesbank is loath to give the impression that it can be pressured by the French," Lamers said.

Meanwhile, a stronger dollar in Europe would boost the greenback against the yen. Analysts said this development would complicate perceived efforts by Japanese and U.S. officials to restrain the dollar near 115 yen.
"There's probably a cap at 115. There's been a basic shift to trying to slow down the depreciation of the yen," said McGee.

U.S. exporters have repeatedly complained the rising dollar hurts their competitiveness and Japanese leaders seem sensitive to the potential fallout over any worsening of the bilateral U.S.-Japan trade gap.
Japan's "Mr. Yen," Eisuke Sakakibara, recently suggested the dollar's rally would not go much further, effectively capping the greenback at 115 yen.

On Thursday, Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau, briefly sent the dollar above 113 yen with televised comments that the market would determine the proper trading level, denying reports that he preferred a range of 108 to 110.
Early Thursday afternoon, the dollar was trading at slightly over 1.55 marks and 112 yen.
